Butler's referent is certain (Homer, Od. 7.61, has 'with her'): Periboea, 'the youngest daughter of Eurymedon', named in the sentence before. Naming the father keeps Butler's 'daughter' and asserts nothing new. It is the same pronoun-to-antecedent repair the 2026-09-23 screening made in this paragraph ('But Rhexenor left a daughter').

Butler's 'friends' carries the Victorian sense of one's own people, kin (Greek philous, Od. 7.76: 'to see your dear ones and reach your high-roofed house'). Present-day 'friends' excludes family. A typical reader narrows the promise to friends and, with 7.18's 'property ... bondservants ... house', misreads what Odysseus longs for. 'Loved ones' is the current word for the same circle. Earlier in this paragraph Butler's 'when any women are friends of hers' is the current sense and stays, so the paragraph now renders one Butler word two ways by sense. That is a deliberate discrimination to record, like 'raiment' → robes/clothing (Book 8 continuity §6). reason: Butler's 'made themselves perfectly clear' means the gods appeared in manifest, visible form (Greek enargeis, 7.201). Current English hears the idiom 'made themselves clear' (spoke plainly), which loses the ground of Alcinous's argument. The adjudicator proposed 'perfectly manifest'. The lead prefers the plainer 'plainly visible'; Butler's 7.17 has no 'visible' or 'plain', and 'visible' at 7.11 is another paragraph, so the collision rule (same paragraph) is not engaged.
